nba_directive.reason_text: This client is waiting on the Fed before acting, but mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury — not the Fed funds rate — so anticipated cuts are largely already priced in; delivering that education is associated with ~2.4x the odds of a soft-credit pull and fewer than 1 in 20 bankers use it, making it the highest-leverage move here. With a 3.75% rate and $148K remaining balance, the banker must anchor to real dollar savings and a break-even timeline to make the threshold feel already crossable.
nba_directive.recommended_strategy_text:
- Lead with the Fed-vs-mortgage education before anything else
  - Open with: 'Quick thing most people don't know — mortgage rates don't actually follow the Fed rate. They track the 10-year Treasury, and any expected Fed cuts are already priced into today's rates. So waiting for a Fed move may not move your rate the way you're thinking.'
  - This reframe is the door-opener; do not skip it or bury it

- Translate their 3.75% rate into a concrete dollar scenario
  - Pull today's best achievable rate for a conventional refi on a ~$148K balance and compute the new P&I
  - Show the monthly delta vs. their current $777/mo payment in real dollars
  - If today's rate is above 3.75%, be honest — do NOT fabricate savings; instead pivot immediately to the HELOC play below
  - If today's rate is at or below 3.75%, present the monthly savings and move to break-even

- Carry a break-even timeline to neutralize the 'I'll wait' objection
  - Break-even = closing costs ÷ monthly savings (ask ops for a closing cost estimate on a $148K conventional refi)
  - Frame it: 'If break-even is X months and you're staying in the home longer than that, every month you wait is money left on the table'

- Protect the 3.75% first mortgage — do NOT pitch a cash-out refi
  - If the client has any high-rate debt (ask directly: 'Are you carrying any credit card balances or other debt?'), pivot to a HELOC / second lien
  - Frame: 'We can leave your 3.75% first mortgage completely untouched and put a HELOC behind it — credit cards are running 25–30%, so even a higher HELOC rate likely saves you real money on those balances'
  - Quantify against their actual balances once disclosed; do not invent a savings figure

- Anchor to their specific financial pain, not generic equity messaging
  - Ask one direct question: 'What's the main thing you're trying to accomplish — lower the payment, pay off debt, or something else?' Then reframe the loan as solving that named problem

- Secure the next step before closing the text
  - Offer a soft credit pull: 'I can run a soft pull — no impact to your score — and show you exactly what rate you'd qualify for today so you have a real number to compare'
  - Alternatively offer a 10-minute call: 'Takes 10 minutes and you'll know exactly where you stand'
  - Do not go silent after one exchange — if no reply in 24 hours, follow up with the break-even number as the hook
